I wanted to take a moment to share something that has been on my mind for a while, because I think it holds a lesson that goes well beyond our own team and our own industry.

Over the past year, our area managers in the western region have been running short training sessions for ward staff at the hospitals we supply. These are not sales presentations. They are practical, hands-on sessions, usually about twenty minutes long, on how to use our disinfectant and hand-hygiene products correctly and in the right quantities on a busy ward.

The reason we started was simple. Hospitals had been telling us that our products ran out faster than expected, and they assumed the problem was quality or price. When our area managers actually went to the wards and watched, they found it was usage. Staff had never been shown the right dilution or the right amount, so they used too much.

After the sessions, consumption per bed came down by roughly 15%, which you might think is bad for a supplier. In fact, complaints fell sharply, and every one of the eleven hospitals in the programme renewed their contracts this year. Several also asked us to run the sessions at their other sites.

I am very grateful to the area managers who gave up their time to do this, often on night shifts, because that is when many of the newest staff work.

What is one thing your customers might be doing wrong that nobody has shown them how to fix?

I've been meaning to post something for a while, so here goes.

Last spring our theatre teams at North Pennine Health Partnership were cancelling around 9% of planned operations on the day. Each one meant a patient who had fasted, arranged time off and often travelled a long way, being sent home.

When we looked into it with the theatre coordinators, the main cause wasn't beds or staff. It was information. Pre-operative assessments, blood results and equipment requests lived in three different places, and gaps were often only spotted on the morning of surgery.

So we built a simple scheduling view that pulls all three together and flags any missing item five days before the operation, while there's still time to fix it. The theatre coordinators designed most of it on paper before we wrote a line of code.

Six months in, on-the-day cancellations are down from 9.1% to 5.2%. That's 412 operations that went ahead as planned.

I'm grateful to the theatre coordinators and the anaesthetic pre-assessment team, who changed how they work to make this possible.

This is going to be a slightly longer post than usual, because I think the context matters and I want to explain properly how we got here rather than just sharing a number.

Last year at Tessellate Cloud we had a problem that I suspect a lot of engineering teams will recognise. We were having incidents, writing postmortems, assigning action items, and then having more or less the same incidents again a few months later.

When we looked closely, we found that the postmortems themselves were not the issue. They were thorough. The issue was what happened afterwards. Action items went into the general backlog, where they competed with feature work and almost always lost. Nobody was really accountable for closing them, and nobody was checking.

So we made two changes. First, every postmortem action item now has a named owner and a due date, and it goes on a separate board that I review with the team leads every two weeks. Second, any action item that is still open after 30 days is raised in our monthly engineering review, in front of everyone.

The results have been clear. Repeat incidents, meaning incidents with the same root cause as one in the previous six months, went from 14 in the first half of last year to 4 in the first half of this year. Action item closure within 30 days went from 38% to 91%.

None of this was technically difficult; it was about follow-through.

How does your team make sure postmortem actions actually get done?

facts.summary: Every postmortem action item now has a named owner and due date on a separate board reviewed fortnightly with team leads; items open past 30 days are raised in the monthly engineering review
facts.impact: Action items had been lost in the general backlog behind feature work

facts.summary: Repeat incidents (same root cause as one in the previous six months) fell from 14 in H1 last year to 4 in H1 this year
facts.impact: Fewer recurring outages

This summer I achieved something I am extremely proud of on our projects.

Every year, the summer months bring a serious risk of heat stress on site. I decided this year that the usual approach was not good enough. I personally redesigned the working schedule so that heavy manual work moved to the early morning and evening, I introduced mandatory cooling breaks every hour during the hottest period, and I insisted that every site have shaded rest areas with chilled water within a short walk of every work front.

I also introduced a buddy system that I designed myself, in which every worker checks on a colleague during each shift.

The results speak for themselves. Heat-related incidents fell sharply compared with last summer, and we had no serious heat illness cases on any of my sites. Productivity during the summer months was barely affected, which many people told me would be impossible. I believe this is the best heat-safety performance in the region.

I am grateful to the site supervisors and the health and safety team for implementing my plan so faithfully.

I believe this shows what strong leadership can achieve when it refuses to accept the status quo.

I have been meaning to write about this for some time, and I want to set out the background properly, because I think the reasons behind a change are often more interesting than the change itself.

For as long as anyone on the team could remember, our plant managers received their monthly results in the second week of the following month. By then, most of them had already moved on to the next set of problems, and the numbers felt like history rather than something they could act on. In our monthly reviews, we spent more time explaining the past than deciding what to do.

Earlier this year, our team began producing a short flash report for each plant on the third working day of the month. It uses some estimates for accruals and a few items are adjusted later. But it is accurate enough to show the plant managers where they stand on material costs, scrap and overtime while there is still time to respond.

The plant managers have used it more than we expected. Two of the four plants changed their overtime planning within the first few months, and overtime costs across the plants have come down noticeably since. The full close still happens as before, and the differences between the flash report and the final numbers have been small.

The credit belongs to the plant accountants, who agreed to work to an earlier deadline, and to the plant managers, who were willing to trust estimates.

How early do your operations teams see their numbers?

I am proud to say that I have transformed transaction monitoring at Lumen Pay, delivering what I believe is one of the most efficient monitoring frameworks in the payments industry.

So, product stuff. Here's a thing that happened.

We spent most of last year building a population health dashboard at Cadence Health. Twelve charts, filters for everything, beautiful design. Clinic managers told us in every interview they wanted it.

I've worked with a lot of businesses over the years, and every one teaches me something.

Last year, a restaurant group in Dubai asked me to help them launch a points-based loyalty app. Their competitors all had one, and the founder felt they were falling behind.

Before building anything, we spoke to forty of their regular guests. Almost none of them wanted points. What they valued was being recognised: a table they liked, a server who remembered their order, a heads-up when a new dish arrived.

So instead of an app, the group trained floor managers to note regulars' preferences in the reservation system and gave each restaurant a small monthly budget to surprise regular guests. The total cost was a fraction of the app's quote.

Nine months on, the share of guests who visit three or more times a quarter has risen from around 18% to around 27%. The operations director, who ran the rollout, now reviews regulars' feedback weekly with every restaurant manager.

Sometimes the most useful thing a marketer can do is talk the client out of the obvious answer.

What does loyalty actually look like for your customers?

facts.summary: Interviewed 40 regular guests of a restaurant group before building a loyalty app; almost none wanted points, they valued being recognised
facts.impact: Avoided building the wrong loyalty programme

facts.summary: Instead of a points app, floor managers record regulars' preferences in the reservation system and each restaurant has a small monthly budget to surprise regulars, at a fraction of the app's quoted cost; rollout run by the operations director

facts.summary: Nine months on, guests visiting three or more times a quarter rose from around 18% to around 27%

I want to share an idea that has worked well in my practice, and I want to take the time to explain where it came from and why I think it works, because I believe the reasoning is as useful as the idea itself.

Anyone who has advised families for long enough knows that the most dangerous moments are not the ones you plan for. They are the moments when headlines are frightening and a client calls wanting to change everything at once. In those moments, it is very hard for anyone, advisor or client, to think clearly. Emotions take over, and decisions made in a hurry can undo years of careful planning.

A couple of years ago, I started asking families to write a short letter to themselves during a calm period. The letter answers three questions: what are we investing for, what would we be tempted to do when things feel uncertain, and what do we want our future selves to remember. We keep the letter in their file, and when they call during a difficult week, we read it together before discussing any changes.

The effect has been noticeable. The number of urgent calls asking to make major changes during volatile periods has fallen considerably among the families who wrote letters, compared with before. More importantly, the conversations we do have are calmer and more thoughtful.

Two of the junior advisors I work with have now adopted the practice with their own clients.

What do you do to help clients make decisions they won't regret?

facts.summary: Families write a letter to themselves in a calm period answering three questions (what we are investing for, what we would be tempted to do when uncertain, what our future selves should remember); it is read together before any changes in a difficult week
facts.impact: Helps families avoid hurried decisions that undo long-term plans

facts.summary: Urgent calls requesting major changes during volatile periods fell considerably among families who wrote letters; conversations are calmer

I've been reflecting on a project we recently finished, and I want to walk through it in some detail, because I think it illustrates something that applies well beyond this particular client and this particular category of spend.

Our client, a mid-sized consumer goods company, was buying corrugated packaging from fourteen different suppliers across its plants. Each plant had built its own relationships over the years, and each one had good reasons for its choices. On the surface, everything looked fine. Prices were broadly in line with the market, and service was acceptable.

When our team pulled together the full picture, though, it became clear that the company was paying for its fragmentation. They were using more than 300 box specifications, many of them differing only slightly, and none of the suppliers was large enough in their business to offer meaningful volume pricing.

We worked with the plant managers and the procurement team to cut the specifications to around 90, and then ran a competitive process that consolidated the spend with four suppliers. The expected annual savings are about $6 million, and the first plants to switch have seen no change in service levels.

A senior associate on our team led the specification work, which involved hundreds of conversations with plant staff about why each box existed. That was the hard part, and she did it with real patience.

I think the lesson is that sometimes the biggest savings come not from negotiating harder but from simplifying first.

Where is complexity quietly costing your organization money?

facts.summary: Client bought corrugated packaging from 14 suppliers using 300+ box specifications; a senior associate led work with plant managers and procurement to cut specifications to around 90
facts.impact: Simplification made volume pricing possible

facts.summary: Competitive process consolidated packaging spend with four suppliers; expected annual savings about $6M; first plants switched with no change in service levels

I want to share some reflections on a part of our transformation work that rarely gets attention, because I think it's one of the most important things a transformation team can do, and one of the least glamorous.

Large banks accumulate technology the way old houses accumulate furniture. Every system was bought or built for a reason, and few are ever switched off, because switching off a system means finding every process, report and colleague that quietly depends on it. Nobody wants to be responsible for discovering the one thing that breaks.

Over the past eighteen months, a small team from technology, operations and risk has worked through our application estate system by system. For each one, they asked three questions: who uses it, what would break if it disappeared, and where else that need could be met. They interviewed users, traced data flows and, where it was unclear, switched systems off for a weekend to see who noticed.

So far, they have decommissioned 14 applications. Together, these saved around £3 million a year in licences, hosting and support, and removed several systems that our risk team had flagged as hard to keep secure. Not a single customer-facing service was affected.

I am grateful to the team, and particularly to our colleagues in risk, who were partners in this rather than gatekeepers.

Transformation is often described in terms of what we build. I think it should be measured just as much by what we are brave enough to switch off. What would you switch off first?
